To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the three countries we have studied, France, Mexico, and China, all faced a common challenge in the global economy in the 1980s and 1990s, namely, the rise of a new international division of labor (NIDL) in which production of manufactured goods became increasingly dispersed across borders.
, after 1980, China, France, Mexico, and the United States all chose to engage the world economy in new ways, but the domestic effects of these choices were quite dissimilar in the four cases.
, as a result of their leaders' global strategies, France and China became more corporatist, while Mexico became more pluralist.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why the global economy, and the internationalization of the state, have had such different impacts on labor movements across the three countries under investigation.
the question of why, in the late twentieth century, the same global economic pressures and the same state responses to those pressures produced very different outcomes in the three states.

the question: Why did countries that were similarly situated globally, and that acted comparably at the global level, turn out differently at the domestic level when it came to interactions between unions and state in the late twentieth-century world?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the global economy and its effects are not a unitary force, but rather a set of forces, and that their impact on states and on unions varies by country and by time, and is mediated by a variety of factors.

the global economy, in a period of rapid change and expansion, had a profound impact on all three of these countries, and in all three of these cases the state, as an actor, was crucial to the process of change.
the book is about three countries that, at the outset, were similar in their global choices, but then, at home, diverged sharply in their domestic outcomes, and about how this divergence came to be.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the three countries in the book all faced a similar predicament at the international level, but each responded to that predicament in a different way at home.

the book explains how and why, in the 1980s and 1990s, the global economy's pressures, in combination with the political economies of three states, generated divergent domestic outcomes for labor and the state.
the global economy is not the only thing that matters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the global economy is not the same for all countries, and that it is not necessarily the case that the global economy will be the same for all workers.
the global economy has been a powerful shaper of domestic politics, and that the domestic economy has been a strong shaper of the global economy.
states, even ones that are very similar, can make choices that produce very different outcomes at home.
